flawed_step: A proof would need a tree to have at least Delta(T)+2 leaves. The strongest general bound that can be justified is at least Delta(T) leaves: remove a maximum-degree vertex v, and each of the Delta(T) resulting components contains a leaf of T (or is a leaf neighbour of v). Nothing gives two extra leaves, and the step fails right at the start, for n=2.
counterexample: T = K2 (n=2), vertices {a,b}, edge ab. deg(a)=deg(b)=1, so Delta(T)=1. Both vertices are leaves, giving 2 leaves. The claim requires at least Delta+2 = 3 leaves, but 2 < 3. Another example: the path P3 (n=3) a-b-c. Degrees are 1,2,1, so Delta=2 and there are 2 leaves (a and c), but at least 4 are required. More generally, every path P_n with 3<=n<=7 has 2 leaves and Delta=2, so each one fails.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. K2 has 2 leaves but would need 1+2=3, and every path P_n with 3<=n<=7 has 2 leaves but would need 4. A tree only has to have at least Delta(T) leaves, and paths and stars meet that bound exactly, with no room for two more.
